---
title: Tanner's Bridge
order: 2
status: final
publishedOn: 2026-10-09

The bridge looked smaller in daylight. Ines came back to it at noon, without
the ladder, with the ledger buttoned into her coat and her hands in her
pockets so nobody would see them shake.

The fourth lamp on the south rail was dark. Its glass was clean. Its door was
shut. When she opened it the wick was cold and dry, as if it had never been
lit at all.

She took out the ledger. Last night's page was still there, and so was the
line she had not written: _Lit before the keeper. Flame borrowed -- not from
the river._ Below it, below her signature, the extra line had changed. It now
read: _Not at noon. At the sixth bell._

## The tanners

The tanners who gave the bridge its name had moved upriver forty years ago,
when the city council decided the smell was bad for business. Their sheds
were still there on the south bank, roofless, full of nettles and broken
vats. Ines walked through them because there was nowhere else to walk.

In the last shed, on a beam above the door, someone had carved a row of
marks. Six hundred and twelve short lines, she guessed, before she had even
counted them, and one more at the end, deeper than the rest, as if the knife
had been pushed in hard.

She counted them anyway. She was right.

## The sixth bell

At the sixth bell Ines stood on Tanner's Bridge with her ladder and her
striker and her ledger, and watched the fourth lamp on the south rail light
itself.

It did not happen quickly. A pale point appeared at the tip of the wick, like
frost forming on glass, and grew until it was the size of a fingernail, and
then stopped. White. Still. Exactly where it had been the night before.

"All right," said Ines, to the lamp, to the bridge, to whoever was keeping a
second ledger in a roofless shed. "All right. Let's see what you owe."

She opened the book to a clean page and began to write.
